paper_title: SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. Project page: https://damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench

Project page: damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench 1. Introduction Robot policies trained from demonstrations are largely evaluated on benchmarks in which objects remain stationary until robot contact [25, 28]. Manipulating moving object requires the robot to adjust the timing and location of contact to the objects speed. Recent studies report that visionlanguage-action (VLA) models struggle with moving objects [46] and examine temporal motion cues [14], inference latency [44], and physical prediction [49]. However, it remains unclear whether these policies adapt their actions to object speed when that speed can be inferred from past frames. Answering this question requires evaluating success rates across speeds to reveal speed-dependent failures and across diverse manipulation skills so that the findings are not tied to few tasks. Each task must also be solvable at the tested speeds so that failures reflect policy limitations rather than task infeasibility. Existing moving-object benchmarks rarely provide all three. Those with larger task sets report success rates at no more than three speeds or provide no per-speed results; those reporting more speeds do so for at most four tasks. Few also check during task construction that an expert solves every task at several speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench (Speed-Wise Evaluation of Embodied Policies), simulation benchmark for movingobject manipulation on conveyor belt. We use conveyor because we can set its speed while keeping the rest of the scene fixed, it supports many manipulation skills, and its motion is visible in the camera images. The benchmark contains 80 conveyor-belt tasks in 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 speeds from 0.10 to 0.40 m/s, with constant speeds in the main protocol and within-episode speed changes in an acceleration setting. To isolate the effect of speed, each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds, and the training demonstrations span the full speed range. To ensure that failures reflect the policy, scripted expert solves every task at four speeds spanning the range, and each task has static counterpart that checks whether it can be learned with stationary object. We fine-tune six VLA models and two video-based world-action models [20, 48]. For each model, we compare the current frame alone with the current frame plus two past frames and evaluate both policies on every task at every speed. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds with or without past frames, as the policies tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed. Measuring success at 13 speeds makes this pattern visible, whereas averaging over speeds hides it. small network on the optical flow between two frames 0.1 apart estimates the belt speed with mean absolute error of 0.010 m/s. Past frames, however, raise the mean success rate by 1040 percentage points for three models and by at most one point for the other five. Linear probes on the fine-tuned policies show that the belt speed is most linearly decodable from these three (R2 = 0.860.99 at the action module), whereas the other five reach at most R2 = 0.58 and gain little from past frames. The speed is useful once policy has it: on 20-task subset, adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and an image-based speed adapter recovers most of this gain. In 720 real-conveyor trials, past frames raise FastWAMs score slightly more than π0.5s, as in simulation, and adding belt speed input raises π0.5s score from 31 to 80, and to 66 when the adapter estimates the speed. We will release the code, demonstrations, and evaluation protocol. We evaluate eight VLA and world-action models with and without past frames on every task at every speed, showing that six of them peak at intermediate speeds and tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed. Using linear probes and speed-conditioned policies, we find that past frames help only the three models from which the belt speed is most linearly decodable, and that speed estimated from the images keeps most of the gain from ground-truth speed input. 2. Related Work Benchmarks for moving-object manipulation. Dynamic grasping benchmarks such as DGBench [4] and DQ-Bench [23] vary target speed for single manipulation skill. Larger suites broaden task coverage: DOMINO [14] includes 35 dynamic tasks and static counterparts, DynaGrasp-32 [6] contains 25 movingobject tasks, LIBERO-Industry [36] covers industrial transfer workflows, and LIBERO-Dynamic [33] evaluates 40 LIBERO tasks at three speeds. These studies do not report dense speed-wise success-rate curves across their full task sets. Benchmarks with more speed levels use them on few tasks and to study other factors: VLALagBench [44] uses nine speeds on four tasks to study inference latency, and Figure 2. One task per skill category (16 categories; task counts in parentheses). Triplets show scripted-expert episodes at 0.40 m/s; time runs left to right. Crops follow the object; arrows show belt direction. AHEAD [37] uses four speeds in one conveyor scenario to evaluate its predictive world model. In contrast, SWEEPBench measures how the success rate itself changes with speed, at 13 belt speeds across 80 tasks in 16 skill categories (Tab. 1). Visual history and motion representations. In behavior cloning, observation history can lower performance because the policy learns to copy its own past actions from it [9, 10, 43], and recent VLA methods add dedicated history mechanisms [21, 24, 26]. MoveBench [50] argues that VLAs trained on single frames are structurally blind to temporal dynamics. For moving objects, DynamicVLA [46] succeeds more often with an earlier frame, whereas DOMINO finds little benefit from raw-frame history on 10-task subset and instead combines optical flow with future-state prediction. DynaWM uses observation history in world model that regenerates VLA action chunks. Motion can also be given to policy explicitly, as frame differences [42], optical flow [34], or point traces [51]. Another route to motion is video pretraining [17, 45]: Cosmos Policy [20] and Fast-WAM [48] adapt pretrained video generation models for control, and Fast-WAM retains video prediction during training without generating future frames at test time. These studies examine history within their own methods. We instead compare VLA and world-action models using the current frame alone or the current frame plus two past frames, and measure the effect at each belt speed. As DynamicVLA does, we feed past frames through each models own image input, without past actions, so SWEEP-Bench measures what standard fine-tuning extracts from visible motion. Probing and speed conditioning. Linear probes test whether variable can be decoded from intermediate features [1]. However, decodability alone does not show that model uses that information [13, 15, 16], so we relate speed probes to changes in success rate caused by visual history and explicit speed input. Conditioning policy on physical parameters estimated from recent observations has precedents in online system identification [47] and rapid motor adaptation [22], and DynamicWAM [27] conditions world-action model on image-plane velocity from optical flow. Our image-based speed adapter follows this pattern and measures how much of the gain from ground-truth speed remains when speed must be estimated. 3. SWEEP-Bench SWEEP-Bench evaluates manipulation success rates on 80 conveyor-belt tasks in 16 skill categories at 13 constant belt speeds (0.100.40 m/s). We use ManiSkill 3 [39] with Franka Panda arm beside the conveyor. Further benchmark details are provided in the supplementary material. 3.1. Task Suites and Demonstrations Task design. Fig. 2 shows one representative task from each of the 16 skill categories. Categories group tasks by the main action their instruction asks for, inspired by DROID [18], which measures task diversity by instruction verbs. Each task has language instruction, simulatordefined success condition, and scripted expert that uses the objects pose and velocity to generate demonstrations. To ensure that each task is solvable at the tested speeds, we include task only if its expert succeeds in at least 80% of evaluation episodes at each of four representative speeds: 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, and 0.40 m/s. 3 Static counterpart. Every task also has static counterpart with the belt stopped and the object initially within reach. We treat it as separate task that checks whether policy can learn the manipulation with stationary object, since its initial object pose and success condition may differ. Environment. Demonstrations and evaluation episodes draw from 185 backgrounds, including indoor scenes from ReplicaCAD [38], ArchitecTHOR [11], and RoboCasa [28], as well as plain table. We also randomize the platform material (39 options), lighting, the object (668 across all task sets), belt direction, the entry point (within 0.10 m), and exterior camera positions (up to 5 cm per axis). The policy receives 224 224 image tiling three exterior cameras and 224 224 wrist image at 20 Hz. Episodes last at most 15 s. Demonstrations. For each of the 80 tasks, we collect 200 successful scripted-expert demonstrations at belt speeds drawn uniformly from 0.100.40 m/s (20 in each of ten equal-width bins; 16,000 in total). Like person picking from conveyor, the expert reaches for an object as soon as it comes into view, so it grasps slow objects earlier on the belt than fast ones. For 40 of the tasks, we also collect 200 demonstrations each on an accelerating belt (Sec. 3.2), with an acceleration drawn uniformly from 0.05 to +0.05 m/s2 per episode (8,000 in total). 3.2. Controlled Belt Speed and Visual Motion Cues In the main evaluation, the belt runs at constant speed during each episode. The randomized factors of Sec. 3.1, such as the background, do not depend on v, and for each task and episode index we reuse the same draws at all 13 speeds. The belt moves objects through friction, so they can slip or turn when the robot touches them, and lifted object no longer moves with the belt. The belt texture scrolls at speed v, so the speed is visible on the belt itself as well as in the objects motion. faster belt brings the object to the robot sooner and keeps it in view for shorter time; we treat both as part of the effect of speed. In the acceleration setting, the belt speed changes at constant rate while the object is within 0.5 of the robot, reaching 0.25 m/s when the object passes the robot. 3.3. Speed-Wise Evaluation Protocol The main simulation comparison evaluates policies on all 80 tasks at 13 belt speeds from 0.10 to 0.40 m/s in 0.025 m/s increments. Each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene for every policy. Simulation pauses during policy inference so that the success rate reflects each policys actions rather than its inference latency [3], which depends on model size and hardware. The acceleration evaluation uses the 40 accelerating-belt tasks at {0.05, 0.025, 0, +0.025, +0.05} m/s2, 20 episodes per task, paired across accelerations. For simulated evaluations, let Sv denote the mean success rate across the evaluated tasks at speed v, with each task weighted equally. For the main 80-task comparison, the overall success rate is the mean of Sv across all 13 speeds. To test whether speed-wise curve peaks inside the range, we fit least-squares lines of Sv against separately to the speeds below 0.25 m/s and to those above it (six each), giving slopes βslow and βfast in points per 0.1 m/s, and define the peak score = min(βslow, βfast). > 0 means that the success rate rises on the slow side and falls on the fast side. We say policys success rate peaks at intermediate speeds when the 95% interval of lies above zero. We compute 95% confidence intervals for Sv, policy differences, and by resampling tasks. 4. Experiments Training and real-robot details and further results are provided in the supplementary material. 4.1. Setup Models. The six VLA models are π0.5 [2], π0-FAST [31], OpenVLA-OFT [19], GR00T N1.7 [30], VLA-JEPA [35], and DynamicVLA [46]. DynamicVLA is designed and pretrained for manipulating moving objects. The two worldaction models build on pretrained video diffusion models: Cosmos Policy [20] predicts actions within CosmosPredict2 [29], whereas Fast-WAM [48] adds an action module to Wan2.2 [40]. Training. We build on each models released code (openpi [32] for π0.5 and π0-FAST) and extend it to take past frames. We keep each models recipe and change mainly the batch size and the number of training steps. The speed-band, speed-conditioned, and static-counterpart policies are each fine-tuned on all 80 tasks together and evaluated on 20-task subset. We drew these tasks at random before those experiments, stratified by skill category and by the current-frame π0.5 policys success rate, split into three equal groups, so that the subset spans the difficulty levels of the full set and most of its skill categories. The acceleration experiments use the 40 tasks with accelerating-belt demonstrations, separate set. For acceleration, we also fine-tune π0.5, Fast-WAM, VLA-JEPA, and DynamicVLA with past frames on the accelerating-belt demonstrations, starting from the same pretrained weights as the constantspeed policies. Speed-Wise Policy Evaluation We use SWEEP-Bench to characterize speed-dependent failures and test whether visual history or explicit speed information improves the success rate. How does the success rate vary with belt speed? For six of the eight models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds. Their success rate rises from 0.10 m/s to maximum and falls again by 0.40 m/s, with both current-frame and past-frame input  (Fig. 3)  . For all 12 of these policies, the peak score ranges from +3.2 to +22.9 points per 0.1 m/s, each with 95% interval above zero (Tab. 2). The Figure 5. Hand-labeled outcomes at three belt speeds. Pastframe policies, one episode per subset task. Top: the six models that peak at intermediate speeds (120 episodes per speed); bottom: DynamicVLA and Fast-WAM (40). other two, DynamicVLA and Fast-WAM, do not peak and succeed most at or near the slow end of the range. With past frames, π0.5 and Fast-WAM have similar mean success rates (40.5% and 35.9%), so averaging over speeds hides this difference. The 12 peaked policies fail even at slow speeds, although slower belt leaves more time to act. Slow speeds are solvable, as DynamicVLA and Fast-WAM succeed at 0.10 m/s in 4862% of episodes, more often than any of the 12 policies. As qualitative failure analysis, we labeled by hand the failures of the eight past-frame policies in one episode of each subset task at 0.10, 0.25, and 0.40 m/s  (Fig. 5)  . For the six models that peak, 48% of all episodes at 0.10 m/s fail because the policy acts before the object arrives, and 69% at 0.40 m/s because it acts after the object has passed. In other words, these policies tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Since the expert grasps slow objects earlier on the belt, policy that ignores the speed learns the average timing, which fits mid-range speeds. The peak indeed moves with the training speeds. We fine-tune π0.5, Fast-WAM, VLA-JEPA, and DynamicVLA separately on each of three speed bands, using past frames. All 12 resulting policies succeed most often within their training band and less often than their full-range counterparts outside it  (Fig. 4)  . At 0.40 m/s, π0.5 trained on 0.30 0.40 m/s reaches 39% success rate, compared with 19% for the full-range policy, despite using one third as much training data. Figure 6. For Fast-WAM, Cosmos Policy, and DynamicVLA, moves toward zero: they gain little at their best speed and more at the other speeds, so past frames widen the range of speeds they handle. Unlike the other five models, these three were pretrained on multiple frames, in different ways. Fast-WAM and Cosmos Policy build on video diffusion models (Wan2.2 and Cosmos-Predict2) trained to generate the frames of video together, whereas DynamicVLA was trained to predict actions from temporally separated images of moving objects [20, 46, 48]. VLA-JEPA also learns from videos, but during pretraining its policy pathway receives only an initial observation; future-frame features serve as prediction targets [35]. This distinction is consistent with VLA-JEPAs small history gain: predicting future features alone does not guarantee benefit from observed visual history. Does visual history improve the success rate? We compare current-frame and past-frame policies trained on the same demonstrations spanning the full speed range. Past frames raise the mean success rate by 26.4, 9.6, and 39.5 percentage points for Fast-WAM, Cosmos Policy, and DynamicVLA, respectively (Tab. 2). The speed is less linearly decodable from the other five models: π0.5 reaches R2 = 0.58 in its language model, and π0-FAST, OpenVLA-OFT, GR00T N1.7, and VLA-JEPA at most 0.21. None of these five gains more than one point from past frames (Tab. 2), which suggests that past frames help little when the speed is hard to decode from the policy. Even before fine-tuning, the speed is far more decodable from the pretrained models of Cosmos Policy (CosmosPredict2, R2 = 0.84), Fast-WAM (Wan2.2, 0.57), and DynamicVLA (0.77) than from those of the other five (at most 0.08). These results suggest that pretraining on multiple frames, from video [17] or from moving-object demonstrations, helps policy act on the speed. Belt-speed input helps, even when estimated. Beltspeed input improves all four models tested, and speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. On the 20-task subset at seven speeds (0.100.40 m/s in steps of 0.05), ground-truth speed input raises the mean success rate of the past-frame policies by 34, 20, 12, and 15 percentage points for π0.5, Fast-WAM, VLA-JEPA, and DynamicVLA  (Fig. 7)  . π0.5 and VLA-JEPA gain from the speed even though past frames do not raise their success rate. Can policies learn to handle an accelerating belt? To test whether policies can learn to handle belt speed that changes within an episode, we fine-tune π0.5, Fast-WAM, VLA-JEPA, and DynamicVLA on accelerating belts and compare each with its constant-speed policy on these 40 tasks  (Fig. 8)  . Conclusion We introduced SWEEP-Bench, benchmark of 80 conveyor tasks at 13 belt speeds. Many fine-tuned policies tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed, and our results suggest that past frames widen the speed range only for those pretrained on multiple frames. An estimated speed recovers most of the gain that policies obtain from the ground-truth speed. 8 Limitations. Due to computational constraints, each policy is fine-tuned once, which may introduce some noise into our results. The eight models differ in architecture and training data, so we cannot attribute the gain from past frames to pretraining on multiple frames alone. The simulator pauses during inference, so inference latency does not affect the success rates. Other motion inputs, such as optical flow, might help policies that gain little from raw frames.

The conveyor is fixed box, so the simulator never moves the belt surface. Instead, before every physics step (t = 0.01 s), we apply friction force to each object in contact with the belt.
